hints: Sort the three structures by acidic functional group first, think which type loses $H^+$ more easily, a $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group or an $\text{OH}$ attached directly to the ring.
For the two carboxylic acids A and C, look at what is different next to the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group and how electronegativity pulls electron density.
Link stronger acidity to weaker $\text{O-H}$ bond and more stable negative anion after $H^+$ is lost.
walkthrough:
Spot the two different acid families**
Look closely, A is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, a carboxylic acid. C is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CHClCO}_2\text{H}$, also a carboxylic acid. B is $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$, a phenol with $\text{OH}$ directly on the ring. As a rule you can trust, carboxylic acids are much stronger acids than phenols, so B will be least acidic.

Decide between the two carboxylic acids**
Both A and C lose the $\text{OH}$ proton from $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ to give $\text{CO}_2^-$. C has a Cl atom on the carbon next to the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group. Chlorine is very electronegative, so it pulls electron density toward itself through the sigma bonds. This is the electron withdrawing inductive effect.

Link withdrawing to stability and strength**
Picture the anion $\text{RCO}_2^-$. If electron density is pulled away from the $\text{CO}_2^-$ by Cl, the negative charge is spread out and stabilised. A more stable anion means the forward dissociation is more favoured. It also means the original $\text{O-H}$ bond is more polar and weakened. So C with Cl plus $\text{C=O}$ has the greatest stabilisation, A is next, B with only phenolic O is least. That gives $\text{C > A > B}$.

Final answer: C > A > B, most acidic to least acidic.
C is strongest as electronegative Cl and $\text{C=O}$ withdraw electron density, weakening the $\text{O-H}$ bond and stabilising the carboxylate anion.
A is a carboxylic acid so stronger than phenol B, B is weakest as phenol with only one electronegative O to stabilise the phenoxide anion.

hints: To put a $\text{CH}_3$ group onto benzene by electrophilic substitution, think which small molecule can supply $\text{CH}_3^+$ with help from a strong Lewis acid catalyst.
walkthrough:
Recognise the alkylation pair**
You want $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$. That is Friedel-Crafts alkylation. The $\text{CH}_3$ fragment comes from a halogenoalkane, most simply $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$, and the $\text{Cl}$ is pulled off by the Lewis acid catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$ to generate the real electrophile.

Final answer: compound: chloromethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$
catalyst: aluminium chloride, $\text{AlCl}_3$

hints: Remember $\text{AlCl}_3$ accepts a chloride ion to become $\text{AlCl}_4^-$, leaving the carbon fragment behind as a positive ion.
walkthrough:
Write the Lewis acid base split**
Think of $\text{AlCl}_3$ as electron deficient. It grabs $\text{Cl}^-$ from $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$. So $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{AlCl}_3$ gives the large anion $\text{AlCl}_4^-$ plus the methyl carbocation $\text{CH}_3^+$. Check atoms and charge: one $\text{Al}$, four $\text{Cl}$, one $\text{C}$ and three $\text{H}$, overall neutral to $1- + 1+$ balanced.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{AlCl}_4^- + \text{CH}_3^+$

hints: Start with the rich pi cloud of benzene acting as nucleophile toward $\text{CH}_3^+$, think where the first curly arrow begins and ends.
Recall the intermediate temporarily loses aromaticity and carries a positive charge delocalised in the ring.
Consider how aromaticity is restored by loss of a ring proton, and what base removes it to give the final products.
walkthrough:
Electrophilic attack by the ring**
Picture benzene with its delocalised pi cloud above and below the ring. That cloud reaches out to the empty p orbital on $\text{CH}_3^+$. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the ring and pointing to the $\text{CH}_3^+$, forming a new $\text{C-C}$ bond. One carbon of the ring becomes tetrahedral.

Draw the charged intermediate**
You now have a cyclohexadienyl cation, often called the arenium ion. The ring has $\text{CH}_3$ and H on one carbon, and the positive charge is delocalised over the other five carbons. Aromaticity is broken here, so this species is high in energy.

Restore aromaticity**
A base, for example $\text{AlCl}_4^-$, pulls off the hydrogen from the same carbon that gained the $\text{CH}_3$. Draw a curly arrow from that $\text{C-H}$ bond back into the ring to remake the pi system. The products are methylbenzene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{H}^+$. The ring is aromatic again, which is the driving force.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\text{CH}_3^+$ to form positively charged arenium intermediate; intermediate with $\text{CH}_3$ attached and $+$ in ring; curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond back into ring to reform aromatic $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ + $\text{H}^+$

hints: Recall the vigorous oxidant that converts an alkyl side chain on a benzene ring fully to a $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group with heating.
Balance the change $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ using $[\text{O}]$ atoms, counting O and H on each side.
walkthrough:
Choose the side chain oxidant**
An alkyl group attached to benzene resists mild oxidation, but hot alkaline potassium manganate(VII), $\text{KMnO}_4$, with heating, oxidises the whole $\text{CH}_3$ side chain up to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Acidification afterwards gives benzoic acid.

Write the [O] equation**
Using $[\text{O}]$ to represent oxidising power: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + 3[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Check it, left has three extra O atoms, right has two in $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ plus one in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Hydrogens balance, $8$ on each side.

Final answer: reagent: hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$
equation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + 3[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Think opposite directing behaviour, $\text{CH}_3$ pushes electrons and directs ortho and para, while $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ withdraws and directs meta.
walkthrough:
Apply directing rules**
Methyl is electron donating and activating, so it directs the incoming $\text{NO}_2^+$ to the 2 and 4 positions relative to $\text{CH}_3$. Draw benzene with $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{NO}_2$ ortho or para to each other. The $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group is electron withdrawing and deactivating, so it directs meta. Draw benzene with $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ in 1,3 positions.

Final answer: From methylbenzene: 2- or 4-nitromethylbenzene (ortho or para $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NO}_2$). From benzoic acid: 3-nitrobenzoic acid (meta $\text{HOOC C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NO}_2$).

hints: To turn a primary aromatic amine into a diazonium salt, recall the unstable nitrogen reagent made in situ and why the mixture must be kept ice cold.
walkthrough:
Name the diazotisation mix**
Primary aromatic amine $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NH}_2$ to diazonium $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ needs nitrous acid $\text{HNO}_2$, generated from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid. Keep the temperature between $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ in an ice bath because the diazonium salt decomposes if warmed.
Final answer: reagents: $\text{HNO}_2$ (from $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$); conditions: $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $10^{\circ}\text{C}$

hints: Think what happens when a diazonium salt is warmed in water, which small gas leaves and which group replaces the $\text{N}_2^+$.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the diazonium salt**
If you let $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ warm with water above $10^{\circ}\text{C}$, nitrogen gas bubbles off and $\text{OH}$ from water replaces the diazo group. That gives the phenol $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$. No extra reagent beyond $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and heat is needed.
Final answer: warm to above $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (hydrolysis gives $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$ + $\text{N}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$)

hints: For azo coupling, join the two rings through a $\text{N=N}$ bridge, think which species provides the $\text{N}_2^+$ end and which provides the activated phenol end.
Recall the pH and temperature that keep the diazonium ion stable and make the phenol reactive enough to couple.
walkthrough:
Build the azo linkage**
Coupling joins the diazonium nitrogen to the phenol ring. Write $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N=N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_3(\text{CH}_3)\text{OH}$. The $\text{N=N}$ bridge links the two aromatic rings, one bearing $\text{CH}_3$ from the diazonium part, the other bearing $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{OH}$ from the phenol part, coupling para to the $\text{OH}$ if free.

Give the coupling conditions**
Keep the mixture cold, $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $10^{\circ}\text{C}$, so the diazonium ion does not decompose. Use alkaline conditions, aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, which converts the phenol to phenoxide, a much stronger activated ring for electrophilic attack by the diazonium ion.

Final answer: structure: $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N=N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_3(\text{CH}_3)\text{OH}$
conditions: $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ (alkaline)
